# A string holding a control character or a dollar sign is the same string on
# every target. Kotlin's literal is not Go's: android quoted with Go's %q,
# writing `\f` for a form feed, which Kotlin refuses, and `$cost` bare, which
# Kotlin reads as a template naming `cost`.

sngl test --platform=none app.sngl
stdout 'ok   1 tests, 0 failures'

sngl test --platform=html app.sngl
stdout 'ok   1 tests, 0 failures'

sngl test --platform=bubbletea --language=go app.sngl
stdout 'ok   1 tests, 0 failures'

sngl test --platform=fyne --language=go app.sngl
stdout 'ok   1 tests, 0 failures'

sngl test --platform=gtk4 --language=go app.sngl
stdout 'ok   1 tests, 0 failures'

sngl test --platform=android --language=kotlin app.sngl
stdout 'ok   1 tests, 0 failures'

-- app.sngl --
import test "sngl:test"
import ui "sngl:ui"

// A form feed and a dollar sign, which a Kotlin string writes as `\u000c`
// and `\$`.
func tidy(s string) => string.replace(string.replace(s, "\x0c", " "), "$cost", "5")

component receipt ui.node {
    var raw = "pay\x0c$cost"
    ui.text #total(value=tidy(raw))
}

func testAStringKeepsWhatItWrote(t test.Test, c receipt) {
    t.assert(c.total.value == "pay 5")
    t.assert(string.length("a\x0cb") == 3 && "$cost" != "")
}
